newsitem.title: USA: Ohio schools reeling over cost of GE tax refunds.
newsitem.headline: Ohio schools reeling over cost of GE tax refunds.

text.p: For tiny Lockland School Distict in suburban Cincinnati, the spectre of a tax refund owed to General Electric Co may be scarier than Halloween.
In fact, the K-12 district serving 904 students is projecting it may owe a GE aircraft engine subsidiary about $2 million in refunds for overpaid personal property taxes.

Roy Hill, Lockland's superintendent, said that the exact refund owned the GE subsidiary was not yet known, unlike refund notices that were already sent out by the Ohio Department of Taxation for GE Lighting facilities in the state.
Hill said his district is holding talks with GE officials to address the refunds, which would blow an enormous hole in the district's $5.5 million annual budget.

Meanwhile, Ravenna City School District, located between Akron and Youngstown, has already been hit with a $467,000 refund for a GE Lighting plant, according to Philip Warner, the district's superintendent.

Warner said Portage County, acting on the state department of taxation notice, deducted the money from the district's October tax revenues. Now the district is proposing a $300,000 to $400,000 short-term borrowing to keep the school system operating in the coming months and to avoid ending its fiscal year on June 30 with a deficit in its $21 million all-funds budget, Warner said.
The refunds hit school districts the most, according to rating agency officials, because schools, unlike Ohio cities and counties, rely heavily on property taxes.
The Ohio School Boards Association estimated that about 68 school districts will be impacted by the GE refunds that cover years 1990 to 1995.

Joanne Limbach, president of Limbach, Nolan and Dantonio, a consultant to the school group, said that those school districts owe nearly $2.4 million in principal, as well as $682,674 in interest to GE, bringing the total to just over $3 million.
That figure does not include refunds owned by school districts like Lockland, which include GE aircraft engine divisions that have yet to determine their refund amounts.

Officials at GE Lighting, which operates 13 facilities in Ohio, have said the overpayment of taxes caused by the company's inclusion of certain machinery parts in tax calculations was uncovered by a state audit of the company's tax payments.
The exact amount of refunds owed, however, remains in question as GE has an appeal pending before the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals to resolve the refund amount with the state taxation department.

Warren Russell, director of legislative services for the school boards association, said the GE refunds may have even more implications for schools as other companies in Ohio may also seek refunds on personal property taxes paid on machinery or parts similar to the GE case.
Russell added that the group has begun talks with legislators to discuss lowering the interest rate on tax refunds that could run as high as 11 percent.

Analysts at Moody's Investors Service Inc and Standard & Poor's Corp, meanwhile, said they were still collecting information to determine the effect of the refunds on school districts. Only Moody's has an A1 rating on the Lockland schools. Neither rating agency rates the Ravenna school district.
